new_statements.quote: [1972, p.25] Stress is predictable. The primary stress occurs on word initial syllables and secondary stress on following alternate syllables. The final secondary stress in three, five and seven syllable words is optional. Words of from one to seven syllables have been found. e.g. Two syllable words. /"ga.nok/ all come ... Three syllable words. /"ko.uat.'ŋâ/ his father in law ... Four syllable words. /"kâm.bi.'am.ŋâ/ his liver ... [1976, p.27] Stress is predictable. The primary stress occurs on word initial syllables and secondary stress on following alternate syllables. The final secondary stress on three five and seven syllable words is optional. Words of from one to seven syllables are commonly found. Primary stress in the examples below is indicated as ", secondary stress as '.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog initial stress (initial stress for 2- to 6-syllable words); adds secondary stress on alternate syllables, the optional final secondary in odd-length words, attestation up to 7 syllables, and the phrase intonation contours. The 1976 revision ('This paper supersedes previous papers produced in 1968 and 1972') repeats the 1972 statement almost verbatim, and Southwell's 1992 OPD ( p.3, not a listed work) says 'The primary stress occurs on word initial syllables.'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable: primary stress on the first syllable of every word; secondary stress on the following alternate (odd-numbered) syllables, i.e. 3rd, 5th, 7th. Examples run from 2 to 7 syllables: "ga.nok, "ko.uat.'ŋâ, "kâm.bi.'am.ŋâ, "u.lu.'lun.sei.'ko, "mo.li.'ziŋ.gâ.'ba.bot, "sâk.u.'râp.niŋ.'aŋ.gâ.'ren 'to our ancestors'. Phrase-level intonation is separate: a question phrase has a stressed low-pitch nucleus followed by rising pitch; a statement phrase has a stressed high-pitch nucleus followed by falling pitch (1976 p.28-29; 1972 p.26).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternate syllables after the initial (3rd, 5th, 7th); the final secondary stress in three-, five- and seven-syllable words is optional.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors call stress fully predictable. No weight sensitivity, no lexical exceptions mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1976 revision states that it specifically covers the Central, Andâ River (No. 2) dialect of Komba, 'but the statement is generally applicable to the other two dialects' (Guamâ River No. 1 and Puleng River No. 3, which differ only in stop consonants). The 1972 version's data come from the village of Muin (Koŋe) in the Kabwum Sub-district; the 1972 sentence-types paper also draws on the Koŋe area. Both are Komba proper (ISO kpf, komb1273), not Selepet or Timbe.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant', rule initial (initial stress) rests on Southwell 1992 OPD p.3, quote confirmed verbatim in the copy downloaded now. The fuller primary source, Southwell & Southwell 1972 'Phonemes and Orthography of Komba' sec. 5.3 (downloaded now, read from the scan), says 'Stress is predictable. The primary stress occurs on word initial syllables and secondary stress on following alternate syllables', with marked examples of 2-7 syllables all showing initial primary and secondaries on syllables 3, 5, 7 (final odd secondary optional). This confirms fixed initial primary stress and refines the record with a secondary-stress rule and word-length range; no weight sensitivity, no lexical exceptions, no tone mentioned. If anything the 1972 statement ('predictable', no exceptions) would support strict fixed: initial syllable rather than merely dominant, but no reclassification of the primary-stress class is n
